assumptions: USD million. Disposal qualifies as discontinued under fictional policy. Taxes assigned separately; disposal gain included in discontinued result; no other items.

evidence.text: Continuing revenue 900; continuing operating costs 720; interest 30; tax 30.
Disposed division revenue 180; costs 165; sale proceeds 95; carrying amount of disposed net assets 70; disposal tax 8; operating tax 3.
Division operating cash flow 12; no cash in disposed entity, sale costs or other cash movements. Prior-year continuing profit 105.

qas.question: Calculate current continuing pretax profit.
Find continuing profit after tax.
What gain arises from the division disposal?
qas.answer: 95−70=25 million USD.

qas.question: Determine discontinued profit after both taxes.
Compute total net income including discontinued operations.
Why is the 95 sale receipt not operating profit from the division?
qas.answer: It is proceeds from disposal; only the 25 difference over carrying amount enters disposal gain, separately from trading profit.

qas.question: Can total operating cash flow of the whole business be found?
qas.answer: No. Continuing operations cash flow is absent.

qas.question: Would comparing 149 to prior-year continuing profit 105 be like-for-like?
qas.answer: No. Current 149 includes discontinued result; comparable continuing profit is 120.

assumptions: USD million. Toy equity award expense = grant-date fair value × estimated awards expected to vest × elapsed service fraction, with cumulative catch-up. No market conditions, tax or cash settlement.

evidence.text: Grant 1 million awards at $12 grant-date fair value; service period three years.
End of year 1 expected vesting 90%; expense recognized 3.6 million. End of year 2 estimate decreases to 75%.
No awards exercised or settled; current market price $20, not used in stipulated expense measurement.

qas.question: What total grant-date value applies before forfeiture estimates?
qas.answer: 1 million×$12=12 million USD.

qas.question: Calculate cumulative expense required after two years.
qas.answer: 12×.75×2/3=6 million USD.

qas.question: What expense is recognized specifically in year two?
qas.answer: 6−3.6=2.4 million.

qas.question: If the 90% estimate had remained, what year-two expense would have been recorded?
Why is the current $20 price not substituted for $12 here?
qas.answer: The toy policy fixes grant-date fair value for equity awards and updates estimated vesting only.

qas.question: Does the expense reduction establish cash savings in year two?
qas.answer: No. Equity compensation is noncash under the facts.

qas.question: Can actual eventual share dilution be determined?
qas.answer: No. Final vesting, exercise or settlement and total ordinary shares are missing.

qas.question: Does the estimate change prove management manipulated profit?
qas.answer: No. It shows a change in expected vesting; no evidence of improper intent or estimation process.

assumptions: USD million equivalent at current rates. Toy net open position = currency assets−liabilities+net forward receivable. Currency moves 10% against reporting currency; linear value sensitivity, no tax or basis.

evidence.text: EUR assets equivalent 500; EUR liabilities 350; forward net payable EUR equivalent 100.
GBP assets equivalent 160; GBP liabilities 220; forward net receivable GBP equivalent 20.
EUR depreciates 10%; GBP appreciates 5%. No other currency positions or accounting classification.

qas.question: Calculate the net EUR open position.
qas.answer: 500−350−100=+50 million USD equivalent.

qas.question: Calculate the net GBP open position.
qas.answer: 160−220+20=−40 million USD equivalent.

qas.question: Estimate EUR shock profit or loss.
qas.answer: Long 50×−10%=−5 million USD.

qas.question: Estimate total currency value change across both shocks.
qas.answer: EUR −5 plus GBP short −40×5%=−2, total −7 million.

qas.question: Why does a short GBP position lose value when GBP strengthens?
qas.answer: Liabilities net of assets and hedges increase in reporting-currency value, producing a loss.

qas.question: Can gross EUR assets 500 be treated as the full unhedged exposure?
qas.answer: No. EUR liabilities and the forward payable offset most of the gross asset exposure.

qas.question: Can the calculation establish daily cash collateral calls?
qas.answer: No. Forward collateral arrangements, settlement dates and liquidity terms are missing.

qas.question: Can the total value change be assigned exactly to profit versus OCI?
qas.answer: No. Accounting designations and classifications are absent.

assumptions: USD million; 2 million units annual demand unchanged. Buy price $8/unit; make variable cost $5/unit; incremental fixed cash cost 4 million; existing unavoidable overhead 3 million common. No tax.

evidence.text: Supplier purchase cost $8 per unit. In-house variable cost $5 per unit; demand 2 million units.
Manufacturing adds fixed annual cash cost 4 million and requires equipment investment 10 million today.
Existing overhead 3 million unavoidable in either choice. No quality, capex life or discount rate disclosed.

qas.question: Calculate annual outsourcing purchase cost.
qas.answer: 2×8=16 million USD.

qas.question: Calculate relevant annual internal manufacturing cash cost.
qas.answer: 2×5+4=14 million USD; exclude unavoidable common overhead.

qas.question: Find annual cash operating savings from making internally.
qas.answer: 16−14=2 million USD.

qas.question: At what annual volume in million units do relevant operating costs break even?
qas.answer: 4/(8−5)=1.3333 million units.

qas.question: Why exclude common overhead from the incremental decision?
qas.answer: It is incurred under either choice, so it cancels in the difference.

qas.question: Does the positive annual saving justify the 10 million investment on its own?
qas.answer: No. Investment horizon, discounting, maintenance and residual value matter.

qas.question: Can the proposal's NPV be calculated?
qas.answer: No. Equipment life, discount rate and future investment cash flows are unspecified.

qas.question: Can we conclude internal production meets supplier quality standards?
qas.answer: No. No quality or reliability measures are supplied.

assumptions: USD million. Toy deferred acquisition cost (DAC) policy: qualifying costs capitalized, amortization recognized; specified impairment separate. No other changes.

evidence.text: Opening DAC asset 70; acquisition cash costs 50, of which 40 qualify for capitalization.
Annual DAC amortization 25; impairment 8. Earned premium 300 and claims expense 190.
Other underwriting expense 45, excluding all acquisition-related expense. No tax or investment income.

qas.question: Compute immediate acquisition expense on current cash costs.
qas.answer: 50−40=10 million USD.

qas.question: Determine closing deferred acquisition cost asset.
What total acquisition-related expense enters the current period?
qas.answer: 10+25+8=43 million USD.

qas.question: Calculate underwriting profit after all disclosed costs.
Why is 50 paid not equal to acquisition expense of 43?
qas.answer: Some current spending is capitalized, while amortization and impairment consume existing assets.

qas.question: Does impairment of the DAC asset imply a new cash payment?
qas.answer: No. It reduces carrying amount and profit but is noncash under the policy.

qas.question: Can underwriting cash flow be determined from these expenses?
qas.answer: No. Premium collections, claim settlements and other payments are absent.

qas.question: Can the remaining amortization schedule be inferred from closing DAC?
qas.answer: No. Cohort service periods and amortization assumptions are not given.

assumptions: USD million; electricity MWh in thousands. Battery charges 100 thousand MWh at $40/MWh; round-trip efficiency 85%; all delivered electricity sold at $75/MWh. Variable discharge cost $5/MWh; fixed costs 1 million. No other cash operating costs.

evidence.text: Charge 100 thousand MWh, buy price $40; efficiency 85%.
Sell all delivered electricity at $75/MWh; variable discharge cost $5/MWh.
Fixed cash cost 1 million; battery capex 20 million, life/degradation and future prices not specified.

qas.question: How much electricity is delivered after storage losses?
qas.answer: 100×.85=85 thousand MWh.

qas.question: What cash revenue comes from discharge?
Calculate cash gross spread after charging and variable discharge cost.
Find operating cash surplus after fixed costs.
qas.answer: 1.95−1=.95 million USD.

qas.question: Why is comparing $75 sale price with $40 charge price alone insufficient?
qas.answer: Only 85% of input energy is delivered and there are operating costs; spread must account for energy loss and cost.

qas.question: Does the stated efficiency imply zero battery degradation?
qas.answer: No. Round-trip energy efficiency and capacity degradation are different measurements.

qas.question: Can the 20 million investment's IRR be determined?
qas.answer: No. Useful life, future cycling, degradation, price spreads and terminal cash flows are missing.

qas.question: Can accounting depreciation be computed?
qas.answer: No. The depreciable life and residual value are absent.

assumptions: USD million. Toy FFO = ordinary net income + property depreciation − property sale gain. AFFO here = FFO−recurring maintenance capex−straight-line rent adjustment. No other adjustments.

evidence.text: Ordinary net income 80; property depreciation 45; property sale gain 25 included in net income.
Maintenance capex cash 20; straight-line rent adjustment 6 increases accounting rent over cash.
Cash dividends 70; no complete operating cash-flow statement, development capex or share count.

qas.question: Compute FFO according to the disclosed definition.
qas.answer: 80+45−25=100 million USD.

qas.question: Calculate the specifically defined AFFO.
qas.answer: 100−20−6=74 million USD.

qas.question: Find dividends as a percentage of this AFFO.
How much AFFO exceeds the cash dividends?
qas.answer: 74−70=4 million USD.

qas.question: Why does FFO remove the gain on property disposal?
qas.answer: Under the stipulated definition it excludes disposal gains from the recurring-property performance proxy.

qas.question: Does positive AFFO mean the company has 74 in free cash at year-end?
qas.answer: No. AFFO is an adjusted performance metric and not a complete cash-flow or balance measure.

qas.question: Can AFFO per share be calculated?
qas.answer: No. Ordinary share count is missing.

qas.question: Can this payout ratio alone establish dividend sustainability?
qas.answer: No. Debt maturities, development capex, leasing needs and future AFFO are unknown.

assumptions: USD million. Contract base freight rates fixed; surcharge is 70% of fuel-cost increase relative to baseline, recognized in revenue. Volumes and all nonfuel costs unchanged.

evidence.text: Baseline revenue 300, fuel expense 60, other operating expense 190.
Fuel expense rises to 90. Contract permits surcharge equal to 70% of incremental fuel expense; collected in full.
No tax, capex or other changes. Future customer response and renegotiation not supplied.

qas.question: Calculate baseline EBIT.
qas.answer: 300−60−190=50 million USD.

qas.question: Determine contractual fuel surcharge.
qas.answer: (90−60)×.7=21 million USD.

qas.question: What revised revenue is recognized?
qas.answer: 300+21=321 million USD.

qas.question: Calculate revised EBIT.
qas.answer: 321−90−190=41 million USD.

qas.question: Why does revenue rise while EBIT falls?
qas.answer: Only 70% of the 30 fuel increase is passed through; the remaining 9 reduces EBIT.

qas.question: Would excluding the surcharge from revenue but leaving all fuel expense give a comparable EBIT measure?
qas.answer: No. That would remove a genuine recovery while retaining its related cost; use consistent treatment.

qas.question: Can we forecast customer volumes after repeated surcharge increases?
qas.answer: No. Demand response and contract renegotiation are not supplied.

qas.question: Can the new EBIT determine CFO?
qas.answer: No. Cash timing of other operating items, taxes and working capital are missing.
